title: The Enterprise Migration Crisis
summary: CloudMigrate is a cloud migration platform for enterprise IT teams.

Q1.text: A Fortune 500 client's migration has stalled: assessment shows 200 workloads ready, but the client's IT director says they can only commit to 3 more in Q1. The client threatens to cancel. What do you do first?

choices.text: Diagnose whether the bottleneck is internal resourcing or technical readiness
choices.reveal: Internal resourcing: the client's IT team has 4 engineers split across 3 competing projects. Technical readiness is fine.
choices.because: The bottleneck could be headcount or technical issues — diagnosing which saves wasted effort.

choices.text: Escalate to the client's CIO to unblock the IT director
choices.reveal: The CIO overrules the IT director and commits the full team — but the 3-engineer cap was realistic, not a blocker. The schedule slips when reality hits.

choices.text: Offer a 25% discount to extend the contract
choices.reveal: The discount is accepted — but the client still only commits 3 workloads. Price wasn't the constraint.

choices.text: Survey the client's stakeholders about their concerns
choices.reveal: The survey surfaces 7 different concerns from 7 stakeholders — some want faster migration, some want more testing. Signal is diluted.

Q2.text: The bottleneck is internal resourcing — the client has 4 engineers split across 3 projects. What do you do?

choices.text: Ask the client to re-prioritize one project to free up engineers
choices.reveal: The client re-prioritizes — but it delays their security patch rollout, which the security team escalates to the CIO. The migration is saved but creates a new internal conflict.
choices.because: This is the strongest move based on the evidence available.

choices.text: Propose a co-managed model where your engineers shadow theirs
choices.reveal: Two of your engineers are assigned to shadow — but the client's change management process requires internal sign-off, so co-managed doesn't fully unblock.

choices.text: Reduce scope to match the team's available capacity
choices.reveal: Scope is reduced to 3 workloads — but the client sees this as failure to deliver on the promised 200. Trust erodes.

Q3.text: Seven stakeholders have seven different concerns. How do you get clarity?

choices.text: Interview the top 3 stakeholders in priority order to understand their core constraint
choices.reveal: IT director: headcount allocation; security lead: more testing gates; cloud architect: different target architecture. Three distinct concerns, each with a different solution.
choices.because: Priority-ordered interviews surface the actual constraints without getting lost in the noise of seven perspectives.

choices.text: Host a workshop with all 7 stakeholders to align on priorities
choices.reveal: The workshop runs 4 hours — no alignment emerges. Speed, security, cost, and architecture don't converge in a single room.

choices.text: Draft a communication plan addressing each stakeholder concern
choices.reveal: The communication plan is thorough — but it addresses concerns without resolving them. The migration schedule still has no additional commitment.

Q4.text: The real constraints are: headcount allocation, security testing gates, and architecture mismatch. These pull in different directions. What's your strategy?

choices.text: Present a prioritized roadmap: fix headcount first, then security gates, then architecture
choices.reveal: Headcount frees 3 engineers, security gates add 2-week delays per workload, and architecture rework defers 40 workloads to Q2. The migration accelerates and the client sees the full dependency chain.
choices.because: A prioritized roadmap that addresses each constraint in order and shows downstream delays is the only path that resolves all three.

choices.text: Negotiate a contract amendment to scope down to 100 workloads
choices.reveal: The amendment is proposed — but the client sees scope reduction as admitting failure. Legal teams spend 3 weeks negotiating, and the schedule doesn't improve.

choices.text: Assign your own engineers to handle security testing and architecture
choices.reveal: Your engineers handle testing — but the client's security team rejects externally produced artifacts. The work has to be redone internally.

Q5.text: You offered a discount and escalated to the CIO — neither worked. The client still commits only 3 workloads. What's the real issue?

choices.text: Investigate the client's internal politics and project dependencies
choices.reveal: The IT director is protecting their team's bandwidth for a concurrent ERP upgrade. The migration isn't a priority because the ERP project has executive sponsorship and the migration doesn't.
choices.because: Neither price nor escalation moved the commitment — the real constraint is internal prioritization the client hasn't acknowledged.

choices.text: Present a phased delivery plan with clear milestones
choices.reveal: The phased plan is presented — but without addressing the ERP project's priority, the client still won't commit more workloads.

choices.text: Bring in a solution architect to re-validate the migration approach
choices.reveal: The architect re-validates — but the migration approach was never in question. The client knows it will work; they just won't prioritize it.

Q6.text: The real issue is internal prioritization — the client's ERP project has executive sponsorship and your migration doesn't. What do you do?

choices.text: Help the client build a business case that elevates the migration to executive visibility
choices.reveal: You help craft a business case showing the migration unlocks $2M in infrastructure savings and reduces risk. The CIO elevates it above the ERP project, and the client commits 10 workloads for Q1.
choices.because: Elevating the migration to executive visibility addresses the actual constraint — the client's internal priority imbalance.

choices.text: Accept the 3-workload commitment and optimize the delivery
choices.reveal: You accept 3 workloads — but the business case for the other 197 workloads remains buried. The migration completes 3 workloads and the client renews for a small expansion only.

choices.text: Pull your engineers off the migration and reallocate to other clients
choices.reveal: Your engineers are reallocated — but the client sees the reduced engagement as abandonment. The relationship deteriorates and the contract is not renewed.

Q8.text: You've secured executive visibility for the migration and the client commits 10 workloads for Q1. But the client's ERP project is still consuming engineering bandwidth. What do you do?

choices.text: Negotiate a temporary dedicated engineer from the ERP project for the migration
choices.reveal: A dedicated engineer is borrowed from ERP for 4 weeks — the 10 workloads move into the testing phase. But the ERP project slips its deadline by 2 weeks.
choices.because: A temporary resource loan from the prioritized ERP project is the move that accelerates the migration without a permanent conflict.

choices.text: Wait for the ERP project to finish before starting the migration
choices.reveal: The ERP project runs another 6 weeks — the client's migration commitment window passes. They've moved on to other priorities.

choices.text: Use your own engineers to do the migration work
choices.reveal: Your engineers take over — but the client's security team requires internal sign-off on every migration artifact. The external work has to be redone by the client.

Q9.text: The migration is in the testing phase with a temporary engineer borrowed from ERP. The client's security team demands additional penetration testing. What do you do?

choices.text: Negotiate a fast-track security review in exchange for additional security documentation
choices.reveal: The fast-track is negotiated — you produce the documentation, security does a focused review in 3 days. The migration passes testing and goes live on schedule.
choices.because: Trading documentation for a fast-track review acknowledges the security concern while respecting the timeline — both sides get something.

choices.text: Reject the additional testing as outside the agreed scope
choices.reveal: The rejection stands — but the security team withholds sign-off, and the migration is blocked at the final gate. The client escalates to their board.

choices.text: Agree to the full penetration test and extend the timeline
choices.reveal: The full test is scoped at 3 weeks — the migration goes live, but 2 months late. The client questions the timeline discipline.

Q10.text: The migration passes testing and goes live. But the client's internal success metrics are conflicting: engineering says uptime is 99.9% (success), but business users report intermittent slowdowns. What do you measure?

choices.text: Break down the uptime metric by the specific workloads that business users rely on
choices.reveal: The breakdown shows 3 workloads have 2-second+ latency spikes during peak business hours. Those 3 workloads are the ones business users interact with daily. The 99.9% uptime is averaged across workloads that business users never touch.
choices.because: The aggregated uptime metric hides per-workload performance — business users don't care about the average, they care about their workload.

choices.text: Trust the engineering metric of 99.9% uptime and close the project
choices.reveal: The project is closed — but business users continue reporting slowdowns. The client escalates to your VP of Customer Success, and the relationship sours.

choices.text: Run a customer satisfaction survey about the migration
choices.reveal: The survey shows mixed satisfaction — high on technical reliability, low on user experience. But the survey doesn't pinpoint which workloads cause the slowdown.

Q11.text: Three workloads have 2-second latency spikes during peak hours — the ones business users rely on. What do you do?

choices.text: Profile those workloads in production to find the bottleneck
choices.reveal: Profiling shows the bottleneck is shared database queries under concurrent access. The database instance is under-provisioned for concurrent access.
choices.because: Production profiling of the specific slow workloads isolates the actual bottleneck — a shared resource, not a code issue.

choices.text: Scale up the database instance immediately
choices.reveal: The database scales up — but latency persists because the issue is concurrent query access patterns, not instance size.

choices.text: Add caching to the three workloads
choices.reveal: Caching is added — latency drops for 2 workloads but the third has dynamic data that can't be cached.

Q12.text: The bottleneck is shared database queries under concurrent access. What's your fix?

choices.text: Implement connection pooling and query-level read replicas for those workloads
choices.reveal: Connection pooling is configured and read replicas assigned. Latency drops to under 200ms during peak. Business users confirm the improvement.
choices.because: Connection pooling and dedicated read replicas address concurrent-access bottleneck specifically.

choices.text: Re-architect the workloads to avoid shared queries entirely
choices.reveal: The re-architecture is scoped at 8 weeks — but the workloads are live and business users depend on them. A rewrite would cause downtime.

choices.text: Schedule a maintenance window to scale the database vertically
choices.reveal: Vertical scaling requires downtime, and the client can't afford a 2-hour outage for business-critical workloads.

Q13.text: The migration is live, latency is fixed, and the client is satisfied. But you discover the 3 workloads were only 20% of the planned 200-workload migration. What do you recommend?

choices.text: Propose a phased plan: batch migrations in groups of 20, with rollback readiness per batch
choices.reveal: The phased plan: 9 batches of 20, each with rollback. Client approves phases 1 and 2, committing to 40 more workloads.
choices.because: This is the strongest move based on the evidence available.

choices.text: Push to commit all 180 workloads at once for efficiency
choices.reveal: The bulk commitment is pushed — but the client's CFO escalates that a single failure could affect all 180 workloads.

choices.text: Commit to migrating 60 workloads over the next quarter with dedicated engineering support
choices.reveal: The 60-workload commitment is accepted — a balanced approach. Client signs for 60% of the remaining scope.

Q14.text: You're planning the next phase of migrations. The client's ERP project is complete. What does the success framework look like?

choices.text: Document the learnings into a repeatable migration checklist
choices.reveal: The checklist captures: pre-migration profiling, resource allocation, security fast-tracking, and post-migration validation. The next 60 workloads migrate 40% faster.
choices.because: Codifying learnings into a repeatable checklist turns a one-off recovery into an efficient process.

choices.text: Run a retrospective with all stakeholders
choices.reveal: The retrospective surfaces 15 feedback points — valuable but broad. Without a checklist, the next phase repeats coordination issues.

choices.text: Scale the team and migrate all remaining workloads simultaneously
choices.reveal: The team scales to 10 engineers — but coordination complexity grows non-linearly. Three workloads fail during cut-over.

Q15.text: The checklist made the next 60 workloads 40% faster. The client asks about managed services for ongoing cloud optimization. What's your recommendation?

choices.text: Propose a managed services retainer scoped to workloads already migrated
choices.reveal: The retainer is scoped to 80 workloads with 24/7 monitoring. Client signs a $120K annual contract — the highest-value upsell.
choices.because: A scoped retainer on already-migrated workloads is the natural upsell — the client has seen the value and trusts the team.

choices.text: Hand off workloads to the client's operations team
choices.reveal: The handoff is executed — but without monitoring, two workloads degrade unnoticed for 3 weeks. The client re-engages for incident response.

choices.text: Offer the entire managed services catalog at a discount
choices.reveal: The full catalog is offered — but the client is overwhelmed by choices and defers the decision.

Q16.text: The client signed the managed services retainer. The contract includes quarterly reviews. What do you establish as the review agenda?

choices.text: A scorecard of workload performance, cost optimization, and security compliance — with remediation items per workload
choices.reveal: The scorecard is presented quarterly — each review identifies 2-3 optimization opportunities. Over the year, cost is reduced 15% and no incidents escape detection.
choices.because: A per-workload scorecard with remediation items turns quarterly reviews into continuous optimization, not status reporting.

choices.text: A high-level report on uptime, incidents, and spend — aggregated across all workloads
choices.reveal: The high-level report is clean — but one workload's cost spike is buried in the aggregate. The client only discovers it during a surprise audit.

choices.text: A presentation of new features and services the client should adopt
choices.reveal: New features are presented — but the client sees them as upsell attempts, not optimization. The managed services relationship becomes transactional.

criteria.label: Letting evidence lead
criteria.guidance: Identify the actual constraint before pushing the process.

criteria.label: Sizing customer impact
criteria.guidance: Ground the decision in what changes for the customer.

criteria.label: Setting the direction
criteria.guidance: Decide which customers to serve first.

criteria.label: Managing risk and trade-offs
criteria.guidance: Name what each path risks — data, timeline, or credibility.

criteria.label: Proving the outcome
criteria.guidance: Define the measure that separates a real fix from activity.

criteria.label: Trade Off Clarity
criteria.guidance: Address this criterion in your decision.
